stories.headline: US shifts military forces to Mideast amid reported planning for post-election Iran strike

claims.text: A person briefed on U.S. and Israel's war planning told NPR that the two countries are preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran.
Any strike is expected after the U.S. midterm elections (Nov. 3) and after Israel's elections next week.
The U.S. is deploying a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East.
Some U.S. personnel are being withdrawn from the region as reinforcements arrive.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recently traveled to Israel to meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
NPR's source said Israel had initially intended to strike Iran in mid-October but held off after President Trump objected.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran is prepared for both diplomacy and war.
Iran is demanding formal control over the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran is demanding withdrawal of U.S. troops from the region.
Israeli security forces in the occupied West Bank detained about 80 people.
Those detained included U.S. Democratic congressional nominee for New York Brad Lander and more than a dozen American rabbis.
NPR's Ruth Sherlock said the war planning could be intended to pressure Iran toward a diplomatic deal.
Ruth Sherlock noted Netanyahu is campaigning to topple Iran's regime.
Ruth Sherlock noted Netanyahu could use the threat of military action to help form a unity government if Israel's election results are unclear.
NPR's Greg Myre said Trump will likely weigh military action only after Nov. 3 to avoid a spike in oil prices before the U.S. midterm elections.
U.S. forces are visibly repositioning in the Middle East—an added carrier, a Pentagon chief's visit to Israel, and personnel rotations.
A source briefed on the planning says both Washington and Jerusalem are preparing for a possible post-election strike on Iran.
The timing is shaped by two separate electoral calendars: U.S. midterms on Nov. 3 and Israeli elections the following week.
Netanyahu has a domestic political need to either show strength against Iran or use the threat of war to build a coalition government.
Iran has signaled openness to both negotiation and conflict.
Iran has made demands (control of the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. troop withdrawal) that neither Washington nor Israel appears willing to meet.
The diplomatic and military tracks are running in parallel with no resolution yet confirmed.

Across the U.S., Israeli, and Iranian sides, each actor's posture appears driven as much by near-term political calendars—U.S. midterms, Israeli elections, Netanyahu's coalition math—as by the underlying strategic dispute.
The planning reported here may be as much a pressure tactic as a fixed decision to strike.
Whether this results in actual military action will likely become clearer only after Nov. 3 and Israel's elections the following week.

In the meantime, watch for further U.S. troop and carrier movements, any shift in Iran's rhetoric or demands, and signs of whether Netanyahu uses the threat of force for coalition-building rather than an actual strike.

stories.headline: GOP presses to expel Ilhan Omar as DOJ probe deepens over name, finances and home raid

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: Homeland Security Investigations agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C. home on Oct. 12.
The search began around 6 a.m. EDT.
15-25 agents were present for the search.
The search lasted for roughly five hours.
Agents left with 17 items.
Items included multiple cellphones, notebooks, a children's Somali-language phrasebook, Omar's passport, and her husband's 1960s camera.
A federal court filing identified Omar under the name 'Ilhan Nur Said Elmi'.
The filing listed 'Ilhan Abdullahi Omar' as an alias.
Omar was born in Somalia.
Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000.
More than a dozen grand jury subpoenas have been issued to members of Omar's family as part of the investigation.
President Trump posted on Truth Social calling on Omar to 'IMMEDIATELY resign,' citing the name discrepancy.
Trump has denied any involvement in the DOJ probe.
Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) told Fox News Digital he plans to pursue Omar's expulsion from Congress if DOJ finds her guilty of immigration fraud.
Expulsion from Congress requires a two-thirds vote of the full House.
A separate DOJ investigation is examining Omar's financial disclosures.
The financial disclosures showed the value of two businesses tied to her husband rising from as much as $51,000 in 2023 to as much as $30 million in 2024.
The financial disclosures were later amended to between $18,004 and $95,000.
No criminal charges have been filed against Omar in connection with either the immigration matter or the financial disclosures.

The story involves two distinct, ongoing federal inquiries into Rep. Ilhan Omar: one tied to possible false statements on immigration and naturalization documents, and a separate Justice Department review of her financial disclosures.
Neither probe has produced charges.
Rep. Ilhan Omar called the raid 'an outrageous abuse of power' and 'weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies.'
Former President Barack Obama said the federal probe was 'so appalling.'
Omar argued President Trump has 'everything to do with' the investigation, citing his 2019 comments calling for her to be 'sent back.'
President Trump said the investigation has 'nothing to do with me' and called Omar 'a disaster.'
Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) said he will demand Omar's expulsion if DOJ finds she is not a citizen or committed immigration fraud.

House Oversight Chairman James Comer (R-Ky.) said the committee's review found discrepancies in Omar's financial disclosures, including a winery tied to her husband that he said shut down 'because of fraud.'
Key facts (the reason for the name discrepancy, the cause of the financial-disclosure swing) remain unresolved.
The dispute is already being used for fundraising by Omar's campaign and the DNC ahead of the midterns.

facts: Homeland Security Investigations agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C. home on Oct. 12, beginning around 6 a.m. EDT with 15-25 agents present for roughly five hours.
Agents left with 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, a children's Somali-language phrasebook, Omar's passport, and her husband's 1960s camera.
A federal court filing identified Omar under the name "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi" and listed "Ilhan Abdullahi Omar" as an alias; Omar was born in Somalia and became a U.S. citizen in 2000.
More than a dozen grand jury subpoenas have been issued to members of Omar's family as part of the investigation.
President Trump posted on Truth Social calling on Omar to "IMMEDIATELY resign," citing the name discrepancy, and has denied any involvement in the DOJ probe.
Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) told Fox News Digital he plans to pursue Omar's expulsion from Congress if DOJ finds her guilty of immigration fraud; expulsion requires a two-thirds House vote.

A separate DOJ investigation is examining Omar's financial disclosures, which showed the value of two businesses tied to her husband rising from as much as $51,000 in 2023 to as much as $30 million in 2024, before being amended to between $18,004 and $95,000.
No criminal charges have been filed against Omar in connection with either the immigration matter or the financial disclosures.
ladder.analysis: The story involves two distinct, ongoing federal inquiries into Rep. Ilhan Omar: one tied to possible false statements on immigration and naturalization documents, triggered by a home search and a court filing listing a different legal name, and a separate Justice Department review of her financial disclosures stemming from a sharp, later-amended discrepancy in reported business assets tied to her husband. Neither probe has produced charges, and officials have not publicly detailed what crime, if any, is alleged in the immigration matter. Expulsion from Congress is a high bar, requiring a two-thirds vote of the full House, and is constitutionally separate from any criminal investigation or citizenship question, which would itself require formal legal proceedings to resolve.

Former President Barack Obama said the federal probe was "so appalling."

Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) said he will demand Omar's expulsion if DOJ finds she is not a citizen or committed immigration fraud.

House Oversight Chairman James Comer (R-Ky.) said the committee's review found discrepancies in Omar's financial disclosures, including a winery tied to her husband that he said shut down "because of fraud."

ladder.steelman: Across both camps, the rhetoric—resignation demands, expulsion threats, and cries of political weaponization—has outpaced the legal record: two separate federal inquiries remain open, no charges have been filed, and key facts (the reason for the name discrepancy, the cause of the financial-disclosure swing) remain unresolved.

stories.headline: Supreme Court allows New Hampshire to bar student IDs at polls

claims.text: On Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a brief, unsigned order staying a federal district court injunction.
The Supreme Court's order cleared the way for New Hampshire to bar student IDs as valid identification for voting in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The underlying law, HB 323, was signed by Gov. Kelly Ayotte in April 2026.
HB 323 took effect June 2, 2026.
HB 323 removed student IDs from the list of documents expressly valid for obtaining a ballot.
After the law took effect, Secretary of State David Scanlan issued guidance instructing local election officials not to consider student IDs even under the state's separate 'catch-all' provision.
The catch-all provision lets voters lacking qualifying photo ID establish identity by other means.
The Coalition for Open Democracy sued, arguing the law and guidance violate the 26th Amendment.
The Coalition for Open Democracy argued the law and guidance impose an unconstitutional burden on voting rights under the First and 14th Amendments.
On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante left the core law in place but issued a preliminary injunction blocking Scanlan's guidance.
Judge Laplante ruled that officials still had to consider student IDs alongside other evidence under the catch-all provision.
The 1st Circuit Court of Appeals declined to stay Laplante's ruling.
New Hampshire's Attorney General's Office asked the Supreme Court on Oct. 15 to stay Laplante's order.
The Supreme Court granted the stay, citing the Purcell principle that federal courts should not alter election rules close to an election.
The Supreme Court referenced a recent Missouri redistricting dispute in its order.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter.
Justice Jackson wrote that Laplante's order addressed misinformation about the state's rules rather than changing them and should not have been disturbed.
The Supreme Court's action is a stay, not a ruling on the merits.
The underlying lawsuit over HB 323's constitutionality continues in the lower courts.
The dispute centers on whether a federal court can modify how a state's voter-ID rules are applied in the final weeks before an election.
The Supreme Court's reliance on the 'Purcell principle' has become a recurring flashpoint in election litigation nationwide.
The Purcell principle was invoked in a recent Missouri redistricting case.

For New Hampshire voters, the practical effect is immediate: student IDs, from high schools or colleges, cannot be used to obtain a ballot or as supplementary evidence of identity in the Nov. 3 midterms.
Voters without a government-issued ID will need another path to verify identity at the polls.
The case now returns to the ongoing merits litigation over HB 323's constitutionality.
This order determines only the rules for the upcoming election, not the law's ultimate fate.
Both the majority and the dissent agree on the goal of avoiding voter confusion.
The majority and dissent disagree on which action — freezing a late court order or letting it stand — better serves that shared goal so close to Election Day.
The underlying constitutional challenge to HB 323 will continue in the lower courts after the midterms.
The student-ID ban's long-term legal status remains unsettled even as it governs the Nov. 3 election.
The case adds to a growing body of Purcell-principle rulings that election-law watchers in other states may cite in future disputes over last-minute judicial intervention in voting rules.

facts: On Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a brief, unsigned order staying a federal district court injunction, clearing the way for New Hampshire to bar student IDs as valid identification for voting in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The underlying law, HB 323, was signed by Gov. Kelly Ayotte in April 2026 and took effect June 2; it removed student IDs from the list of documents expressly valid for obtaining a ballot.

After the law took effect, Secretary of State David Scanlan issued guidance instructing local election officials not to consider student IDs even under the state's separate 'catch-all' provision, which lets voters lacking qualifying photo ID establish identity by other means.
The Coalition for Open Democracy sued, arguing the law and guidance violate the 26th Amendment and impose an unconstitutional burden on voting rights under the First and 14th Amendments.

On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante left the core law in place but issued a preliminary injunction blocking Scanlan's guidance, ruling that officials still had to consider student IDs alongside other evidence under the catch-all provision; the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals declined to stay that ruling.

New Hampshire's Attorney General's Office asked the Supreme Court on Oct. 15 to stay Laplante's order, which the Court granted, citing the Purcell principle that federal courts should not alter election rules close to an election, referencing a recent Missouri redistricting dispute.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter, writing that Laplante's order addressed misinformation about the state's rules rather than changing them and should not have been disturbed.
The Supreme Court's action is a stay, not a ruling on the merits; the underlying lawsuit over HB 323's constitutionality continues in the lower courts.
ladder.analysis: The dispute centers on a narrow but consequential procedural question — whether a federal court can modify how a state's voter-ID rules are applied in the final weeks before an election — rather than on the constitutionality of New Hampshire's student-ID restriction itself, which remains unresolved. The Supreme Court's reliance on the 'Purcell principle,' a doctrine holding that courts should avoid last-minute changes to election procedures to prevent voter confusion, has become a recurring flashpoint in election litigation nationwide, invoked here as it was in a recent Missouri redistricting case. For New Hampshire voters, the practical effect is immediate: student IDs, from high schools or colleges, cannot be used to obtain a ballot or as supplementary evidence of identity in the Nov. 3 midterms, meaning voters without a government-issued ID will need another path to verify identity at the polls. The case now returns to the ongoing merits litigation over HB 323's constitutionality, with this order determining only the rules for the upcoming election, not the law's ultimate fate.
ladder.steelman: Both the majority and the dissent agree on the goal of avoiding voter confusion; they disagree only on which action — freezing a late court order or letting it stand — better serves that shared goal so close to Election Day.
ladder.implications: The underlying constitutional challenge to HB 323 will continue in the lower courts after the midterms, meaning the student-ID ban's long-term legal status remains unsettled even as it governs the Nov. 3 election. The case adds to a growing body of Purcell-principle rulings that election-law watchers in other states may cite in future disputes over last-minute judicial intervention in voting rules.

stories.headline: Trump waives new Russia sanctions as GOP allies warn pressure on Putin is slipping

claims.text: The Graham Act is formally the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.
President Trump signed the Graham Act into law last month.
The Graham Act authorized new tariffs on Russia.
The Graham Act authorized new tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy.
The Graham Act authorized sanctions on Russian financial institutions.
The Graham Act authorized sanctions on foreign entities doing significant business with Russian financial institutions.
Congress included presidential waiver authority in the Graham Act.
Trump invoked the waiver authority over roughly a week to put most of the Graham Act's new Russia sanctions and tariffs on hold.
Trump argued that imposing the Graham Act penalties risks driving Russia away from peace talks.
The Senate passed the underlying legislation by an 86-11 vote, according to Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C.
The administration separately eased existing restrictions to allow more Russian diesel exports onto the market.
The administration paired its waiver decision with separate relief on Russian diesel export restrictions.
In his formal certification to Congress, Trump stated that imposing the Graham Act penalties now 'would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace.'
Trump left open the possibility of imposing the Graham Act penalties later to 'incentivize resolution' of the war.
Trump's waiver does not eliminate sanctions against Russia that predated the Graham Act.
The administration retains authority to revisit the Graham Act's new penalties.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright described the sanctions relief as a 'carrot' intended to encourage Russian de-escalation.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright framed the separate relief on Russian diesel export restrictions as an incentive for de-escalation.
Sen. Katie Britt publicly criticized the administration's decision to waive the Graham Act penalties.
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito publicly criticized the administration's decision to waive the Graham Act penalties.
Sen. Thom Tillis publicly criticized the administration's decision to waive the Graham Act penalties.
Sen. Darline Graham publicly criticized the administration's decision to waive the Graham Act penalties.
Sen. Darline Graham is the law's lead sponsor.
Sen. Darline Graham named the legislation for her late brother.
Brands noted that waiver authority is common in sanctions legislation to give presidents flexibility.
Brands is a foreign policy analyst.
Sen. Katie Britt said she believes Russia is at 'the darkest point' of the war.
Sen. Katie Britt said now is the time to increase economic pressure.
Other Republican critics echoed Britt's view in blunter terms.
Brands said including a waiver in the sanctions legislation was not necessarily a mistake.
The waiver ultimately allowed Trump to avoid imposing the penalties lawmakers sought.
Brands said it is difficult to craft sanctions or tariffs legislation that forces a president to act.
Brands said there are always circumstances in which one might want the flexibility to waive sanctions.
Brands argued that repeatedly declining to use the penalties risks signaling to Putin that Washington's threats lack follow-through.
Brands argued that this potentially reinforces a Russian calculation that Western pressure will eventually fade.
Brands said this dynamic has been visible in Trump's approach to the sanctions bill since it was first proposed in early 2025.
The sanctions bill was first proposed in early 2025.
The dispute now centers on whether keeping those penalties in reserve strengthens Trump's hand with Putin, or diminishes their value if Moscow doubts he is willing to use them.

facts: The Graham Act (formally the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act) was signed into law by President Trump last month, authorizing new tariffs on Russia and major purchasers of Russian energy, plus sanctions on Russian financial institutions and foreign entities doing significant business with them.
The law included presidential waiver authority, which Trump invoked over roughly a week to put most of its new Russia sanctions and tariffs on hold.
The Senate passed the underlying legislation by an 86-11 vote, according to Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C.
The administration separately eased existing restrictions to allow more Russian diesel exports onto the market.

In his formal certification to Congress, Trump stated that imposing the Graham Act penalties now 'would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace,' while leaving open the possibility of imposing them later to 'incentivize resolution' of the war.
Trump's waiver does not eliminate sanctions against Russia that predated the Graham Act, and the administration retains authority to revisit the new penalties.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright described the sanctions relief as a 'carrot' intended to encourage Russian de-escalation.

Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C. — the law's lead sponsor, who named the legislation for her late brother — publicly criticized the administration's decision to waive the penalties.
ladder.analysis:
The Graham Act, signed into law last month, authorized new tariffs on Russia and sanctions on Russian financial institutions, with Congress including presidential waiver authority — a feature Brands noted is common in sanctions legislation to give presidents flexibility. Trump used that authority over roughly a week to hold back most of the law's new penalties, arguing that imposing them risks driving Russia away from peace talks. Sen. Katie Britt said she believes Russia is at 'the darkest point' of the war and that now is the time to increase economic pressure, a view other Republican critics echoed in blunter terms. The administration paired its decision with separate relief on Russian diesel export restrictions, which Energy Secretary Wright framed as an incentive for de-escalation.

Brands, the foreign policy analyst, said including a waiver in the legislation was not necessarily a mistake, noting that it's difficult to craft sanctions or tariffs bills that force a president to act, since there are always circumstances in which one might want the flexibility to waive them. But he argued that repeatedly declining to use the penalties risks signaling to Putin that Washington's threats lack follow-through, potentially reinforcing a Russian calculation that Western pressure will eventually fade — a dynamic he said has been visible in Trump's approach to the sanctions bill since it was first proposed in early 2025.
ladder.steelman: Brands said including a waiver in the sanctions legislation was not necessarily a mistake, even though it ultimately allowed Trump to avoid imposing the penalties lawmakers sought, noting that it is difficult to craft sanctions or tariffs legislation that forces a president to act, since there are always circumstances in which one might want the flexibility to waive sanctions.
ladder.implications: The dispute now centers on whether keeping those penalties in reserve strengthens Trump's hand with Putin, or diminishes their value if Moscow doubts he is willing to use them.

stories.headline: Justice Department opens investigation into Corey Lewandowski

claims.text: The Justice Department has opened an investigation into longtime Trump advisor Corey Lewandowski.
The investigation originated from a criminal referral sent to the Justice Department by the Department of Homeland Security's Inspector General.
Lewandowski served as Trump's first campaign manager during the 2016 presidential race.
Lewandowski was fired in June 2016.
Lewandowski later served as a senior advisor during Trump's 2020 and 2024 campaigns.
Lewandowski served as an advisor to former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.
President Trump said he wants his staff to be honest.
President Trump said dishonest staff 'have to be prosecuted.'
President Trump called dishonesty 'stealing from me as president.'
Adam Trigg, an attorney for Lewandowski, said in a statement that Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation.
Adam Trigg, an attorney for Lewandowski, denied any wrongdoing on behalf of Lewandowski.
The Wall Street Journal separately reported that the DOJ was reviewing allegations of corruption and personal financial gain involving Lewandowski.
Lewandowski responded on X calling the Wall Street Journal report 'anonymous-source, politically driven reporting.'

facts: The Justice Department has opened an investigation into longtime Trump advisor Corey Lewandowski, according to a source familiar with the matter who spoke to Fox News.
The probe originated from a criminal referral sent to the Justice Department by the Department of Homeland Security's Inspector General.
Lewandowski served as Trump's first campaign manager during the 2016 presidential race before being fired in June 2016, and later served as a senior advisor during Trump's 2020 and 2024 campaigns.
Lewandowski also served as an advisor to former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.
Asked by reporters about the inquiry, President Trump said he wants his staff to be honest and that dishonest staff 'have to be prosecuted,' calling dishonesty 'stealing from me as president.'
Adam Trigg, an attorney for Lewandowski, said in a statement that Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation and denies any wrongdoing.

The Wall Street Journal separately reported that the DOJ was reviewing allegations of corruption and personal financial gain involving Lewandowski; Lewandowski responded on X calling the report 'anonymous-source, politically driven reporting.'
ladder.analysis: The Justice Department investigation into Corey Lewandowski originated from a criminal referral sent by the Department of Homeland Security's Inspector General. Asked about the inquiry by reporters outside the White House, President Trump said he wants his staff to be honest, warning that dishonest staff 'have to be prosecuted' and that dishonesty amounts to 'stealing from me as president.' Lewandowski's attorney, Adam Trigg, pushed back, stating that Lewandowski has not been contacted by the DOJ regarding any investigation and denying any wrongdoing. Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that the DOJ was reviewing allegations of corruption and personal financial gain involving Lewandowski, a report he dismissed as 'anonymous-source, politically driven reporting.'
ladder.implications: The investigation's trajectory will likely hinge on whether the DOJ formally contacts Lewandowski and what the underlying DHS Inspector General referral alleges in detail; outcomes could range from the matter being closed without further action to a prolonged federal probe, and public developments may test how the administration handles scrutiny of close allies.

stories.headline: Iran warns US forces as oil tankers damaged and possible attack looms
body: Iran is bracing for a possible new wave of US and Israeli strikes after the US midterm elections on November 3 and Israel's election on October 27, according to Iranian officials and media reports. President Donald Trump posted on October 8 that the US would not attack before the midterms, citing 'productive discussions' with Tehran, but may feel less constrained afterward. The New York Times reported Wednesday that the US and Israel have developed specific plans for a 'short but intensive operation' targeting Iran's nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure, and missile and drone arsenal, aiming to force diplomatic concessions by further weakening Iran's economy.

The Pentagon has instructed US Central Command to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran, Axios reported in early October. Two US aircraft carrier strike groups are currently in the Arabian Sea, with a third, the Theodore Roosevelt, expected to arrive by late November. Trump told Newsmax on October 15 that he was considering a strike on Pickaxe Mountain near the Natanz nuclear complex, where US officials believe Iran may have moved sensitive nuclear material underground. CNN reported the next day that Trump is considering using a Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) bomb, though its effectiveness against underground targets like Pickaxe would be limited.

Iranian officials say they are prepared for another attack and plan to respond with strikes on US bases and energy facilities in the Gulf. Ali Asghar Shafieian, a media adviser to President Masoud Pezeshkian, told DW that while the US has the upper hand in military power and technology, Iran's strength lies in how it deals with crisis. He pointed to the rapid replacement of senior officials killed in previous attacks and the rebuilding of missile and drone capabilities as evidence of Tehran's resilience. Iran has told regional governments that US military bases and critical infrastructure could become targets if neighboring countries assist another US or Israeli operation.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned that participation by regional states would result in a 'decisive and proportionate response.' In a post on X Wednesday, he said Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if it sees strong evidence of a sincere US desire to build trust, but added that if the US chooses war over diplomacy, it will result in an 'even greater strategic failure.' Iran's latest proposal, sent through Qatari mediators, included an offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control in exchange for the US lifting its maritime blockade, releasing frozen assets, and ending military actions. However, the Wall Street Journal reported this week that oil flows through Hormuz are approaching prewar levels as the US military escorts tankers, raising questions about whether Iran's leverage over oil flows is weakening.

Inside Iran, the prospect of renewed fighting comes amid severe economic pressure and growing political polarization. A doctor in Tehran, speaking anonymously, told DW that the economic situation has become extremely bad and that she expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting resumes. A woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters and said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of street confrontations. Tehran-based political analyst Rahman Ghahremanpour told DW that Iran's preparations extend beyond missiles and drones to prioritizing internal security, including confronting armed opposition groups and preventing external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest. 'In the government's asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible,' he said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is trailing in polls ahead of Tuesday's election, has campaigned on a platform of regime change in Iran. He said the new supreme leader is attempting to develop nuclear weapons and that there is only one way to remove the threat: overthrow the regime. Former Israeli military intelligence Iran chief Danny Citrinowicz criticized the strategy, arguing that more attacks will not convince Iran to give up its nuclear or ballistic missile ambitions and that Iran could retaliate with even more severe attacks affecting global markets. NPR reported that a person briefed on the matter said Israel had initially planned a strike for mid-October but the US ruled it out. Netanyahu has denied the reports of war plans.

The Wall Street Journal reported that oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz are approaching prewar levels as the US military escorts tankers.
The Wall Street Journal raised questions about whether Iran's leverage over oil flows is weakening.
Inside Iran, the prospect of renewed fighting comes amid severe economic pressure and growing political polarization.
A doctor in Tehran, speaking anonymously to DW, told DW that the economic situation has become extremely bad.
The doctor expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting resumes.
A woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters.
The woman said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of street confrontations.

Tehran-based political analyst Rahman Ghahrehmanpour told DW that Iran's preparations extend beyond missiles and drones to prioritizing internal security, including confronting armed opposition groups and preventing external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest.
Ghahremanpour said: 'In the government's asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible.'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is trailing in polls ahead of Tuesday's election.
Netanyahu has campaigned on a platform of regime change in Iran.
Netanyahu said the new supreme leader is attempting to develop nuclear weapons.
Netanyahu said there is only one way to remove the threat: overthrow the regime.
Former Israeli military intelligence Iran chief Danny Citrinowicz criticized the strategy, arguing that more attacks will not convince Iran to give up its nuclear or ballistic missile ambitions.
Citrinowicz argued that Iran could retaliate with even more severe attacks affecting global markets.
NPR reported that a person briefed on the matter said Israel had initially planned a strike for mid-October but the US ruled it out.

stories.headline: France braces for weekend protests as PSG game moved and 70,000 officers deployed
body: French authorities are preparing for another weekend of violent protests, deploying 70,000 officers and reinforcing police with troops in a massive security operation. The demonstrations follow some of the worst urban violence in years that erupted on the sidelines of protests a week ago, with rioting and looting sweeping through Paris and other French cities on October 17. The Pittsburgh Steelers are scheduled to face the New Orleans Saints in an NFL regular-season game at the Stade de France on Sunday, about 10km from Place de la Bastille, where Saturday's protests are expected to begin.

Paris Saint-Germain's home Ligue 1 game against Lyon, originally scheduled for Sunday, has been postponed until Monday at 8:30pm following a request by police. The French league announced the decision on Friday, noting that the police had issued a decree prohibiting the staging of the match on Sunday. The postponement means that reigning Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele will miss Monday's awards ceremony in London, where he and several PSG teammates are on the men's shortlist. Defending champion PSG and Lyon were level on 14 points at the top of Ligue 1 heading into the weekend. Toulouse's Ligue 1 home match against Troyes has also been pushed back from Saturday to Sunday at the request of local authorities.

According to Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers, the NFL would have cancelled its first regular-season game in Paris if the situation were unsafe. 'I definitely think that the NFL is alert to what's going on,' Rodgers told a news conference on Friday. 'This game means a lot to the NFL. If it was unsafe, then I'm sure we wouldn't be here.' The Steelers informed fans on Thursday that a fan event in the Bastille neighbourhood would not go ahead. The US State Department issued a security alert on Thursday night, calling on its citizens to avoid demonstrations and areas of unrest. The build-up to the game has also been disrupted by Storm Austen, which prompted Meteo France to issue orange alerts for much of the northwest, including the Paris region. The Steelers cancelled their training session due to bad weather, and the NFL also cancelled a fan event on Friday.

The protests began in late September when high school students in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis demonstrated about the state of their school buildings and teacher shortages, angered by proposed government budget cuts. The protests spread nationwide as public sector workers joined to oppose planned pay freezes, and later widened to include those angry about rising living costs, petrol shortages and fuel prices. Demonstrations have frequently descended into rioting, looting and arson. Similar youth-led protests have begun in Italian cities, with many turning violent. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government approved measures including sending 500 soldiers to Milan and increasing financial liability on parents whose children were involved in vandalism and looting. Under new rules, anyone taking part in a group of at least five people and endangering public safety during protests faces up to five years in prison and a maximum fine of 20,000 euros ($22,460).

In France, a new bill known as 'rioters pay' is being proposed by the government in response to the violent protests. The government is scheduled to debate the draft bill on October 27. If passed, those found responsible for vandalism could be required to pay up to 10,000 euros ($11,200) in compensation. In the case of criminal damage by minors, parents could be held responsible. A provision could also introduce collective civil liability, potentially requiring someone in a group responsible for damage to pay, even if they did not cause it themselves. French President Emmanuel Macron has said that 'nothing justifies' violence and that local officials could ban certain street gatherings if deemed necessary. French authorities have also announced curfews.

stories.headline: Trump staffer Britt McHenry throws drink at fan during NBA game, ejected
body: Britt McHenry, a State Department press adviser and former ESPN reporter, was escorted out of Capital One Arena in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday night after throwing a drink at a fan during the Washington Wizards' home opener against the Milwaukee Bucks. Video obtained by TMZ shows McHenry tossing a beverage at someone in the crowd, and bystanders recorded her exit as she was booed and had rally towels thrown in her direction. McHenry, 40, blew kisses to the crowd as she left.

The confrontation began after a group of men behind McHenry and her male guest began heckling Bucks player Kyle Kuzma and disparaging his fiancée, model Winnie Harlow, according to a source cited by Page Six. The source said McHenry, who had been drinking, turned around and told the heckler to 'ease up,' sparking a verbal dispute. The men then allegedly threw 'misogynistic' insults at McHenry and threw a drink on her, prompting her to retaliate with her own drink, the source added. TMZ's sources said the group behind McHenry made inappropriate and misogynistic comments to instigate her, but did not recall exactly what prompted her to throw the drink.

Video shows McHenry arguing with stadium employees, yelling 'What'd I do?' while staff pointed to the front doors. Page Six's source said both McHenry and the man she fought with were escorted out by stadium staff. However, sources close to McHenry told TMZ that she was not kicked out, but left on her own to go to a bar, while her male guest stayed and met up with her after the game. The Wizards won the game 128-116.

McHenry previously worked as an ESPN correspondent for just over three years before the network suspended her in April 2015 after a video surfaced of her berating a tow truck employee. In that video, she told the employee they had 'no education' or 'skillset,' and said, 'Lose some weight, baby girl.' She was fired by ESPN in April 2017. In an August 2024 podcast, McHenry said the video was 'highly edited' and 'doctored,' but maintained her behavior was justified, saying, 'I will always kinda own it, but I look back, and I don't think that video is that big of a deal.'

After leaving ESPN, McHenry joined Fox News as a commentator and later co-hosted a show on Fox Nation. In December 2019, she sued Fox News and her former co-host George 'Tyrus' Murdoch, alleging he sexually harassed her through explicit text messages and lewd comments, and that the network retaliated after she reported the harassment. Fox News said it had fully investigated her complaints and maintained its actions were appropriate. The lawsuit was settled in July 2021 on undisclosed terms, and McHenry left the network. She now serves as a press adviser at the State Department under the Trump administration.

stories.headline: Moderna-Merck personalized mRNA cancer vaccine reduces melanoma recurrence risk by 42% in pivotal trial
body: A large Phase 3 clinical trial testing a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine from Moderna and Merck has shown that the vaccine, in combination with the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab (Keytruda), reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% compared with pembrolizumab alone over a median follow-up of two years. The results, scheduled for presentation at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress in Madrid, are the first from a Phase 3 trial of an individualized mRNA cancer vaccine and mark a significant advance for the treatment of high-risk melanoma that has been surgically removed.

The trial enrolled 1,137 patients across 157 sites worldwide whose melanoma had been excised but who faced a high risk of the cancer returning. All patients received pembrolizumab for 12 months; some also received the custom-made vaccine, intismeran autogene, which targets up to 34 unique genetic mutations, or neoantigens, from each patient's tumor. At two years, 82% of patients in the combination group were alive and recurrence-free versus 70% in the pembrolizumab-alone group. The combination also reduced the risk of distant metastasis or death by 38%. Overall survival data are not yet mature.

The vaccine leverages the same mRNA platform used in Moderna’s COVID-19 shots, training the immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells bearing those neoantigens. “This is a foundational shift in our approach to cancer,” said Prof. Georgina Long, medical director of the Melanoma Institute Australia and 2024 Australian of the Year, who is scheduled to present the findings. “We can harness the immune system in a more personalized way to reduce the risk of melanoma recurrence or death. This has not been achieved before in the history of cancer drug development.”

Outside experts called the data encouraging but noted limitations. “A significant portion do not respond to the vaccine in the first instance,” said Dr. Jessamy Tiffen of the Centenary Institute, adding that cancer cells may adapt over time. Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, described the results as “really, really good milestones” but emphasized that long-term survival and quality-of-life data are needed. Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said the findings “reinforce our conviction that mRNA has the potential to fundamentally change how we treat cancer.”

The vaccine will not become a standard treatment for years. It must undergo regulatory review and further study, and the results were leaked early on social media, prompting a stock drop for Moderna. The trial’s findings have been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine and will undergo peer review. The drugmakers said it is too early to determine whether the combination improves long-term survival.

stories.headline: Analysis of 2,884 supernovae suggests dark energy may change over time
body: An international research team led by scientists at the University of Queensland’s School of Mathematics and Physics has compiled the largest collection of Type Ia supernovae ever assembled — 2,884 exploding white dwarf stars — and found new evidence that dark energy, the mysterious force driving the universe’s accelerating expansion, may not be constant but instead change over time. The findings challenge a central assumption of the standard model of cosmology and could reshape understanding of how the universe evolves.

The project, described in a paper posted on arXiv, unified three decades of astronomical observations into a single consistent framework. PhD candidate Ryan Camilleri said the team rebuilt decades of measurements by applying updated analytical methods to older data. “Over the years we’ve learned a lot more about how supernovae behave so we’ve been able to go back and apply that improved understanding to older data,” Camilleri said. The researchers also accounted for differences among telescopes, cosmic dust, galaxy masses, and subtle effects such as gravitational lensing. The dataset combines historical supernova measurements with findings from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) published in 2024, along with other cosmic measurements including relic light from the Big Bang and maps of galaxy distribution.

“Instead of confirming the standard model of cosmology which assumes dark energy is fixed and unchanging, we have more evidence that dark energy may change over time,” Camilleri said. Astrophysicist Professor Tamara Davis noted that the DES data from 2024 first hinted at time-varying dark energy, and the new compilation sees a deviation from the standard model in a slightly different direction. Importantly, a separate project — the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) — has also found hints of variations in dark energy through surveys of relic sound waves from the early universe. “So, 2 completely independent measurements have found hints of time variation in dark energy, challenging the standard model that dark energy doesn't change,” Davis said.

Understanding dark energy could have implications beyond cosmic expansion. Researchers believe that learning more about its behavior might help reconcile gravity with quantum physics, two theories that remain incompatible. “All of this research may also hold the clue to explain how gravity and quantum physics fit together,” Davis added. “We know these 2 theories are each immensely successful in their own realms, so if we can figure out how to put them together that would be a huge step in theoretical physics.”

The team plans to expand the dataset as additional observations become available, notably from the Dark Energy Bedrock All-Sky Supernova program (DEBASS), which is identifying hundreds of closer supernovae. Incorporating these nearby explosions will provide further measurements to test whether dark energy truly changes over time. The research builds on decades of work by hundreds of astronomers from projects including the Dark Energy Survey, Foundation Supernova Survey, PanStarrs I, Sloan Digital Sky Survey, Supernova Legacy Survey, Carnegie Supernova Project, and the Center for Astrophysics supernova survey.

stories.headline: Alnylam reports promising early data for Huntington's disease drug brezosiran
body: Alnylam Pharmaceuticals announced Friday that its experimental Huntington’s disease drug, brezosiran (ALN-HTT02), showed promise in an initial Phase 1b study. Patients who received the highest dose saw levels of mutant huntingtin in their spinal fluid fall by 60% or 64% on average, depending on the assay used. The data were presented at the European Huntington’s Disease Network Clinical Research Congress.

The company described the safety profile as “encouraging” and said it plans to launch a placebo-controlled study next year to determine whether the drug can actually slow progression of the disease. Brezosiran is designed to partially silence the mutant gene that drives Huntington’s, a devastating neurological disorder.

“We’re getting high levels of knockdown with good safety and tolerability, and so this is all very, very encouraging,” said Pushkal Garg, Alnylam’s head of research and development, in a statement reported by the company.
Alnylam’s next step will be to confirm the results in a larger, controlled trial, with the goal of demonstrating clinical benefit for patients with Huntington’s disease.

stories.headline: Tesla preps Cybercab 'onslaught' with Dallas launch and multi-city rollout
body: Tesla is preparing to expand its gold Cybercab robotaxi service beyond its home market of Austin, Texas, beginning with a launch in Dallas next month and a rollout to additional cities by the end of this year, Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja said Wednesday on the company's third-quarter earnings call. Taneja framed the push as part of a broader ambition to 'literally take over every part of terrestrial transportation,' adding, 'We're starting with getting people from one place to the other, but we want to basically own transportation of any kind on Earth.' Tesla also said it will begin selling Cybercabs to fleet operators by the end of this year.

Tesla already operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUV in small fleets in Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. A broader Cybercab rollout would set up a sharper competitive fight with Waymo, currently the U.S. robotaxi market leader with more than 4,000 vehicles deployed across more than a dozen cities. Tesla has argued that its Cybercab is cheaper and easier to build, which should let it undercut Waymo and other operators on price — but the company still has to reach real scale outside Austin to prove that point.

Financial details on the robotaxi effort remain murky. Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the new ride-hailing business won't be noticeable in the company's overall financial figures until the second quarter of 2027, 'and probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year.' Tesla also changed how it reports robotaxi activity: its second-quarter shareholder letter included a chart for 'Cumulative Paid Robotaxi Miles' that showed a 36% decline from the first quarter, while the new letter replaced that with 'Cumulative Unsupervised Robotaxi Miles,' a measure of how far the fleet drives whether or not paying riders are aboard. Asked about paid miles, Taneja said the company is 'seeing utilization improving' but offered no specifics.

Taneja praised Tesla's engineering team for producing a vehicle that manufacturing colleagues consider 'one of the easiest products for them to scale in terms of manufacturing,' adding, 'So scaling would not be that much of a challenge.' The harder part, he said, is securing 'all the regulatory approvals' so Tesla can 'start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them.' That echoes Musk's long-standing claim that regulatory approval, not technical progress, is the main barrier to robotaxis. Tesla faces at least one concrete regulatory hurdle: in September, just hours after the Cybercab formally launched in Austin, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an investigation into whether the vehicle complies with federal motor vehicle safety standards. The Cybercab lacks features current standards require, including a brake pedal and side mirrors; NHTSA has proposed removing some of those requirements, but that rule change is likely still months away.

Not every Tesla executive agreed on the bottlenecks. Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president overseeing autonomy, said the remaining constraints are 'not purely regulatory' but 'technology-driven.' He noted the Austin service has been gradually expanding its operating hours — from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., then to 10 p.m. to 11 p.m., and soon to 2 a.m. — and still does not run on highways or in certain conditions, although it has been observed operating in heavy rain in Austin, something Waymo's robotaxis have largely avoided. Elluswamy said Tesla plans to tackle more challenging driving scenarios by the end of this year before scaling further. 'We just want to make sure that there's not a single safety incident. That is our operating principle. And even if there's the slightest possible risk at all, we don't like to take on that risk,' he said.

Taneja's 'terrestrial transportation' comments come after Tesla previously showed a concept version of a multi-passenger vehicle called the 'Robovan,' though it is unclear whether his broader remarks signal work on other kinds of transportation. For now, the near-term focus is proving the Cybercab can expand beyond Austin and reach the scale needed to challenge Waymo, with Dallas serving as the next test market.

Tesla's second-quarter shareholder letter included a chart for 'Cumulative Paid Robotaxi Miles' that showed a 36% decline from the first quarter.
The new letter replaced that with 'Cumulative Unsupervised Robotaxi Miles,' a measure of how far the fleet drives whether or not paying riders are aboard.
Asked about paid miles, Taneja said the company is 'seeing utilization improving' but offered no specifics.
Taneja praised Tesla's engineering team for producing a vehicle that manufacturing colleagues consider 'one of the easiest products for them to scale in terms of manufacturing.'
Taneja said, 'So scaling would not be that much of a challenge.'
Taneja said the harder part is securing 'all the regulatory approvals' so Tesla can 'start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them.'
Musk has long claimed that regulatory approval, not technical progress, is the main barrier to robotaxis.

In September, just hours after the Cybercab formally launched in Austin, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an investigation into whether the vehicle complies with federal motor vehicle safety standards.
The Cybercab lacks features current standards require, including a brake pedal and side mirrors.
NHTSA has proposed removing some of those requirements.
That rule change is likely still months away.
Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president overseeing autonomy, said the remaining constraints are 'not purely regulatory' but 'technology-driven.'
Elluswamy noted the Austin service has been gradually expanding its operating hours — from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., then to 10 p.m. to 11 p.m., and soon to 2 a.m.
The Austin service still does not run on highways or in certain conditions.
The Austin service has been observed operating in heavy rain in Austin.
Waymo's robotaxis have largely avoided operating in heavy rain.
Elluswamy said Tesla plans to tackle more challenging driving scenarios by the end of this year before scaling further.

Elluswamy said, 'We just want to make sure that there's not a single safety incident. That is our operating principle. And even if there's the slightest possible risk at all, we don't like to take on that risk.'
Taneja's 'terrestrial transportation' comments come after Tesla previously showed a concept version of a multi-passenger vehicle called the 'Robovan.'
It is unclear whether Taneja's broader remarks signal work on other kinds of transportation.
The near-term focus is proving the Cybercab can expand beyond Austin and reach the scale needed to challenge Waymo.
Dallas will serve as the next test market.

stories.headline: Microsoft AI diagnostic system beats generalist doctors on hard cases, study finds
body: Microsoft's AI diagnostic system, MAI-DxO, correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a study published Thursday in the journal Science. Using cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, the system was correct 83% of the time, while primary care doctors and general internists working individually with reference materials achieved 36% accuracy. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI's CEO, called the result a step toward 'medical superintelligence.'

MAI-DxO coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors, questioning a patient, ordering tests, and debating a diagnosis. The study's data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft's orchestration system adding gains on top. Microsoft tested DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI's GPT-5 and GPT-5.5. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case; DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. With GPT-5.5, DxO increased accuracy from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. The gains did not show up on emergency department cases, where both GPT-5.5 with and without DxO scored about 85% at a similar cost. DxO helped most on complex cases and with less capable AI models; Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO.

Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch that 'the biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.' Microsoft joins Google and OpenAI in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors. Suleyman, who previously co-founded DeepMind and joined Microsoft to lead its AI unit in 2024, said the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable 'really enormous leaps' and that DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare.

Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Microsoft will evaluate the clinical reasoning capabilities of DxO across different hospital settings. Patients who consent will engage with DxO in parallel with standard treatment, and Microsoft will compare DxO's recommendations against human doctors'. King said, 'We think this will be the biggest study of its kind.' Google published a clinical study alongside Beth Israel in The Lancet this month evaluating its own AMIE conversational diagnostic AI in real-world urgent care visits. Microsoft's study in Science coincides with a manifesto around building medical superintelligence, defined as 'the capacity to surpass the strongest contemporary human-led health systems in medical reasoning and coordination across the full arc of care.' Suleyman said, 'This is the kind of technology that everybody in the world wants,' and that this focus could be a differentiator for Microsoft compared to other frontier labs. Microsoft already sells dictation and radiology tools to clinicians and sees DxO as an expansion to those efforts.
